(Translation.) Here is my main objection to this resolution. I do not believe in this parliament dealing with matters which come within the jurisdiction of the provincial government, and this resolution would be an infringement of that principle. Section 92 of the Union Act of 1807 enacts :
Exclusive Powers of Provincial Legislatures- 92. In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming withing the classes of subjects next hereinafter mentioned.
And subsection 13 :
Property and civil rights in the province.
Therefore, this is a matter of civil procedure, and, as I said, it is not within the scope of this parliament to pass legislation of this sort, and were we t<5 deal with it now, it would be on our part an encroachment upon the rights of provincial legislatures.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put I would like to say a few words in regard to it. I think that the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Fortin) was well advised in bringing the question before the House in the form of an abstract resolution, and I say so, because, when it was introduced into this House last session and the session before, it was reduced to the form of a Bill. It was found to be impossible to frame a Bill which would meet all of the many objections which could be brought against it. The hon. member for Laval seeks to evade all the difficulties by simply passing an abstract resolution, but, if we pass an abstract resolution we will only be face to face with these difficulties. The question which meets us is :	Where is the constitutional power
in this matter ? I held before, and that opinion I have not changed, that parliament has a right to declare that the common
law which prevents the salaries paid by the King from being garnisheed, may be altered. We can do that. I think we can do that and thereby put salaries payable by the King or by the government on the same basis as others, but, that is as far as we can go. Then, comes the question:	Who
is to provide the machinery ? It does not seem that this parliament has any jurisdiction over civil procedure to provide how and in what manner these proceedings shall be enforced.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies).

speechtext: If the matter is within the jurisdiction of this parliament is the procedure incidental to it not within the jurisdiction of this parliament also ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fortin) is quite right that where a general subject such as Insolvency or bankruptcy is referred to this parliament, we can legislate effectively upon it, but I do not see that because the 91st section of the Britsh North America Act says that the fixing and providing for the salaries of civil servants is given to this parliament, that therefore we have the power of determining how and in what manner the creditors can recover if they garnishee. I do not think that is an incidental proceeding. That is a civil procedure in my judgment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Cannot you declare it to be an asset of the creditor, and then would it not come under your jurisdiction ?

I think it is well within the power of this parliament to declare that the common law exemption of this debt from garnishee proceedings should be removed, but when we do that we must leave it to the provinces to deal with the garnishee process. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fortin) thinks it is possible to frame a Bill which would provide the proper machinery
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It was done before.

Yes, but the Bill which was submitted to parliament contained at least a dozen fatal objections and it was withdrawn. I do not believe there is any desire on the part of any one in this House to give an unfair exemption to civil servants, but I ask the hon. member (Mr. Fortin) if there is any real practical grievance existing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Yes.

Then where is the evidence of it ? Have we had petitions praying for this legislation ; have any hon. gentlemen engaged in business expressed the opinion in this House that a great grievance exists ? Did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fortin) listen to the words of wisdom that fell from the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards), who told us as a large employer of labour

in this country, that he found the garnishee law most obnoxious and that the result of it was to throw many workmen out of employment, because their wages being garnisheed their employers would not keep them longer. We have heard from the member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) that so grievous had been the legislation of past years with reference to the property of debtors which was attachable by creditors, that the Manitoba government have been obliged to interfere, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) says that so many exemptions now exist that the sheriff has gone out of business in that province. That does not show a idesire to give greater facilities to the creditor to oppress the poor man, but rather to give the debtor a chance. If we pass a statutory declaration that the salaries of civil servants should be subject to garnishee proceedings, I submit that then each province would have to pass the necessary machinery to give effect to that law. One province might do so and one might not, or a province might make the machinery so intricate for the government that the difficulties would be insuperable. What would be the result of that in the case of the Department of Railways, in which the minister told us he had 9.000 men employed ? The province of Ontario has found it necessary to the practical working of the law, to make an exemption of $25, which as a matter of practice exempts nearly all the employees of the government. Assuming that the provinces can enforce their own law in this regard, how are they going to enforce it as against the central government at Ottawa in the case, for example, of employees in the Yukon, many of whom give orders on the Interior Department for the payment of their salaries to their families ? How can you garnishee these ? Suppose that in British Columbia my department has a hundred men employed on our ships and they are paid monthly, how am I to be informed that the salaries of these men are garnisheed ? What I submit is that instead of passing this resolution, the House might declare that in its opinion each department of government should take steps to ensure that the employees should pay their debts or be discharged. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways says that practice does exist in his department to-day, and that if it is brought to his attention or the attention of his chief officers that an employee persistently refuses to pay his current debts, that man is discharged. It has been stated here that the law works well with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway, and that therefore it would work well with regard to the government, but the answer to that was given by one lion, gentleman who declared that it worked odiously as regards the workmen in these large corporations, because when their salaries are garnisheed they are discharged. These companies say Sir LOUIS DAVIES.
that they cannot be dragged into court week after week and month after month in these garnishee proceedings, and so m self-defence they discharge the men. Would hon. gentlemen ask the government to do the same thing ? In my own department, when a poor sailor man gets into debt and his pay is garnisheed am I to discharge him instanter ? Do the hon. gentlemen want that ? I have great faith in the legal acumen of my legal friend (Mr. Fortin) to find some way out of the difficulty which presents itself, but it seems to me that if you pass a statute removing the exemption, then you will have gone to the extent of your jurisdiction in this parliament, and after that the process by which the salaries can be garnisheed must be left to the different provinces. That would involve us in difficulties so great that we would be very unwise indeed to bring about such a state of affairs.
When we have statements such as that made by so large an employer of labour as the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards), and that made by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) as to the methods which have to be resorted to by employers of labour to escape from the restrictions of the law, I think we may well pause before adopting either the motion or the amendment. In the first place, no grievance has been more than slightly alleged ; no petitions have come from the country for such a law ; and, speaking as a minister of the Crown of four or five years' experience, I am unable to say that in my department any real grievance exists, and I believe my colleagues can say the same. Then why plunge into an experiment of this kind ? I deny that the working of the garnishee process in the case of the great corporations has been such as to encourage us to apply that process to government employees. I think it would be hard on poor men, harsh and unjust ; and if we adopted it, we would probably be compelled to resort to what the Ontario legislature has been compelled to resort to. namely, so many exemptions that the improvement sought to be effected would prove to be practically inoperative.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentlemen who have opposed the resolution which is now before this House have urged an objection which I do not think well founded, and I wish to put on record my views on the question, before the vote is taken on the resolution. It was urged here that the legislation which is embodied in this resolution would prove unworkable and that the time is not opportune for passing it.
The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) has dealt with the question from that standpoint and has quoted clause 92 of the British North America Act in support of his views ; but let me call his attention to clause 91 of the same Act which deals with
the matters to which extends the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. Subsection 8 in which are enumerated the classes of subjects within which these matters come, reads as follows :
The fixing and providing for the salaries and allowances for civil and other officers of the government of Canada.
Since under section 91 of the Union Act, the Dominion government is vested with the j power of providing for and fixing the salaries, the assumption is that no other gov-eminent and no other power can interfere with that matter. Therefore, provincial j autonomy is altogether out of question here, and there is no attempt at encroaching upon the rights of provincial legislatures.
Another objection to the Bill is that there '[DOT] do not exist sufficient grievances to warrant the passing of such legislation. Now, in 1897, a Bili was introduced and discussed at considerable length. During the session of 1898 the same Bill was reintroduced. As early as 1893, the late Mr. Beehard had in-1 troduced a Bill providing that the salaries of public officers and government employees should be attachable. And have we not heard, a little while ago, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. William McCreary) stating that in the province of Manitoba this evil was so prevalent that the government of that province, like the legislature of Quebec, had to bring in a law enacting that the salaries of their officials might be liable to seizure. 1 think it would be but fair to put the creditors of the Dominion civil servants on the same footing with the officials of those provinces.
As matters stand now, no creditor cares to take proceedings against any official of the Dominion government. You may sue them, you may get judgment against them, but what is the use of levying a judgment against a civil servant who has nothing in the world to depend upon but the salary he gets from the government ? No creditor would risk the payment of the judicial costs so long as the judgment he gets remains unsatisfied. But let the House adopt this resolution and then we will provide the best machinery to make this legislation workable and truly effective. Should parliament enact such legislation, it would secure to a creditor the right to recover from the civil servant as readily as he does from any one else.

(Translation.) Would the hon. gentleman tell me how he can reconcile that statement with the views expressed by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies)? I would like him to tell me who has the power to regulate the procedure in the civil courts V Is that power vested in the Dominion parliament or in the local legislatures ? Now, supposing it were within the jurisdiction of the local legislature, would the hon. gentleman be
ready to state that the provinces may issue writs against the Crown ?

(Translation.) This parliament would have to provide the necessary machinery for enforcing and putting the law in motion-in so far as their own officials are concerned.
I know of many civil servants in the service of the government here who, having resided in the province of Quebec and got into debt there, refused to pay their bills, because they know that under the law their salaries were not liable to attachment. Now, were such legislation as is now proposed crystallized into law, those employees could be sued at law. Besides, such legislation would not imply a slur upon the character of the civil servants who were willing to pay their honest debts. It could only affect those dishonest debtors who shirk their honourable responsibilities, and thus bring discredit upon their colleagues.
One of the hon. gentlemen who spoke before me endeavoured to assimilate the case of the government employees with those^ of railway companies, such as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who make it a rule to discharge their officials when a writ of attachment is served in the offices of the company, and when the judgment is not satisfied without the company having to interfere. There is no parity at: all between the two cases. This resolution does not provide for the discharge of public officials who do not pay their debts, but it only asks parliament to give its sanction to the principle that any man in Canada who earns a salary of from two to three thousand dollars a year shall be on a footing of equality before the law with the poor workingman who is earning but a dollar a day. For these reasons, I think that the resolution, introduced by my hon. friend from Laval should pass the House.

0. DUGAS (Montcalm). (Translation.) Mr. Speaker. I have listened very at-tentivelv to the remarks fallen from the hon. gentlemen who have participated in this debate, and I may say that, out of sympathy for the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Fortin), the mover of this resolution, I am very sorry not to be able to support him.
In principle I am in favour of making not only the salaries garnisheeable, but, in fact, everything that belongs to the debtor. I have no sympathy with those laws passed by the provincial legislatures exempting from garnishment a portion of the wages of the workingmen. Those laws, I believe, have defeated the purpose for which they were framed. They have done the working classes more harm than good. I. for one. am a believer in the great principle grounded on equity and justice, in virtue of which the property and goods of the debtor are held as a common pledge by the creditors. Now, if a way could be found out of this trouble,

and if it were possible to apply that old principle to government officials, I would be the first man to approve of such a reform. But, sir, I doubt whether such legislation is within the jurisdiction of this parliament and whether we can pass such a measure without infringing the constitution which governs us.
Hear, hear.

(Translation.) To prove what I say. i need only refer to clauses 91 and 92 of the Union Act of 1867.
Clause 91 deals with the distribution of legislative powers, and enacts in connection with the powers of this parliament that the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects therein mentioned and subsection 8 enacts :
The fixing and providing for the salaries and allowances of civil and other officers of the government of Canada.
The jurisdiction of this parliament, therefore, does not extend beyond fixing and providing for the salaries and allowances of the government officials.
I do not see here anything that enables this House to pass an Act to garnishee the salaries of the servants of the Dominion government.
Section 92 of the Union Act deals with the powers of provincial legislatures, and enacts that in each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects therein enumerated, and among other matters, ' property and, civil rights in the province ' (subsection 13, section 92.) Therefore, under the constitution, this parliament is not empowered to pass a law to enable the 'salaries of civil servants to be garnisheed. Under the Union Act quoted, such a matter is clearly beyond the jurisdiction of this parliament, the legislatures having exclusively the right of making laws in relation to such matter. Therefore in passing such a legislation, we would be encroaching upon provincial autonomy. Moreover, how could such a law be enforced ? I see no way out of this difficulty. The judgments of the courts of the various provinces can only be executed within the limits of tlxe province in which they have been rendered, and exclusively as to the goods and property situate within such province.
The province of Ontario would be the only province Which would reap any benefit from the proposed legislation. The seat of this government being in the province of Ontario, no other orders but those issued by the Ontario courts could reach the government officials.
Now, if in addition to what I have said, we remember this old axiom of the English law, that " The Crown cannot be a "garnishee," the only conclusion that can be come to is that the proposition of the hon. member for Laval cannot be accepted.

The hon. member for Two Mountains (Mr. Ethier) stated, a little while ago, that under section 91 of the Union Act of 1867, this parliament is empowered to enact such a legislation as the one embodied in the proposition of the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Fortin). Surely the hon. gentleman was not in earnest when putting such a construction upon subsection 8. This subsection merely says that this parliament is empowered to deal with the fixing and providing for the salaries and allowances of the officers of the government of Canada ; that is all. This does not imply the rigfit for this parliament to pass a law to enable the salaries of government officers to be garnisheed.
For these reasons, although in principle I am in favour of making the salaries of public employees and the wages of workingmen liable to seizure, and in spite of all esteem and respect I profess for my hon. friend from Laval, I feel in duty bound to vote against the resolution, because such a legislation as the one proposed would be unconstitutional.

Mr. Speaker, I should not have thought it necessary to take part in the discussion this afternoon but for the fact that when the subject came before the House on a previous occasion I deemed it to be my duty to oppose the Bill in which the proposal was then embodied, because I thought that the power of this parliament to deal with the subject was extremely doubtful, to say the least. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies) agreed with me on that occasion in opposing the Bill ; but as the matter is now brought before the House, not in the form of a Bill, which there might be doubt about our power to pass, but in the form of a resolution merely expressing the opinion of the House that the salaries of civil servants should be attachable for the payment of their debts like the salaries of all other classes of the community, I thought we should have the support of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries for this proposal. But it seems that when a Bill is introduced on this subject, it is wrong ; and when a resolution is brought, it is wrong and should have been in the form of a bill. So it seems whichever way we go, we cannot fail to go wrong. The reason I expressed some doubt as to the legislative power of this parliament to deal with the question was that I thought a mistake had been made in the decisions of some of our courts as to the legislative authority of this parliament, notably in the case referred to, that of Le-prohon against the city of Ottawa, where a claim was made on the part of the city authorities to tax a Dominion official in respect of his income. I think it is very important that this matter should be settled, as that decision was closely relevant to the question then before the House and now before the House. I would like very
much if an opportunity could be given to have that question decided in such a way that we might ascertain whether there is to be any privileged class in the community. The reason I objected to the Bill two or three years ago was that it proposed to segregate the civil servants of the Dominion from all other classes by legislating against them in an exceptional way. I think that is wrong ; but I also think it is wrong that Dominion officials or officials of any kind should enjoy privileges and advantages that are not accorded to other people. 1 do not think public officials should be placed in an exceptional position, either adverse or favourable. Places in the public service are very eagerly sought after, as every member of parliament, on this side pf the House at any rate, knows, and X think they should stand on the same footing as any other classes in the community. For that reason, I thought it was desirable that the decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal, I think it was, which seemed to place them in a different position from other classes of the community, should be reviewed. I thought, if it be not presumptuous to say so, that that decision was erroneous, because it seemed to be founded on an entirely false analogy. There was a judgment given a long time ago by Chief Justice Marshall in the United States Supreme Court with reference to the position of officers of the Federal government, and that decision, which was applied by the Ontario Court of Appeal to this class of appointments, was to the effect that if the state legislatures were allowed to tax the salaries of officials of the Federal government, the result might be that the States would have power to destroy an arm of the Federal government. If that was the case, then I presume that was a very proper decision to make, at any rate on political grounds, on which a great many of the judgments of the United States Supreme Court have been founded ; and it was a good judgment, because that was not a desirable condition of things, and was not contemplated by the founders of the Union. That is right enough for the people south of the line ; but my impression is that it has no application to us in Canada, because the Federal government here has a method of protecting itself which the Federal government in the United States has not, and therefore it it not necessary to invoke under our constitution any such principle of safety which might properly be invoked under the constitution of the United States. In Canada, if any legislation is passed by the provincial authorities which, although apparently within the constitutional authority of the provincial legislature, might have the effect of crippling the Dominion service, the Dominion government always has a right to effect a virtual veto of that legislation and to prevent it going into effect. The power of disallowance which we have in our constitution, I think, makes that class of decisions south of the line inapplicable to our conditions north of the line. It was on grounds of necessity that Chief Justice Marshall gave the judgment he did in that matter, and that judgment was the foundation of the decision given here in the case of Leprohon against the city of Ottawa. That political necessity does not exist with us and consequently there is not analogy between that case and our situation. Our provincial legislatures have the right to order a debtor -whether he is a civil servant of the Dominion or not-to pay a certain amount in proportion to his income, and following out that principle I am inclined to think that a provincial legislature would have authority to legislate with reference to this particular subject.
How could a provincial legislature enact a law which would make the government of Canada a party to a suit ?

I was about to refer to that difficulty. If, acting within its legislative authority, the Dominion parliament chooses to pass a Federal Act, that, of course, would override the provisions of any provincial Act. In Nova Scotia, a debtor-whether civil servant or not-may be interrogated as to his means of paying his debts, and the courts have power to order him to pay so much per month or per week. If our provincial courts can make such an order as that, I do not see why they have not the right to take into consideration the fact that the person against whom the order is made is the recipient of a large income from the Federal government, and make an order based on his income. But I understand that there are some decisions in Ontario to the effect that the courts of that province cannot do that.
We can do that in Ontario.

I think that is a good system. As to the abstract proposition that these salaries should be made attachable, by whatever legislature has the power, I do not see why there should be any doubt on that point. I do not see why civil servants should not be placed on the same footing as everybody else.

There is a very general opinion in the country that some Dominion employees cannot be compelled to pay their debts. In this province, I believe, such employees can be brought before the courts and interrogated as to their means and then condemned to pay a certain amount out of their salaries per week or per month, as the case may be. And any civil servant who fails to comply with such an order is guilty of contempt of court and can be sent to jail.

In the province of Quebec, not many years ago, the wages of workingmen were seiz-able to the full amount, but one of our Liberal members from the city of Montreal' managed, after some difficulty, to have the law amended in the local legislature by providing that only one-quarter of the salary of a workingman is seizable, and in such a case the seizure can be made continuous. That was satisfactory to some extent to the creditor, but has worked unfortunately for the debtor. It has enabled creditors to take out suits, pile up costs, turn a man out of employment first, and out of his home afterwards.
With regard to the resolution before the House, I do not think that the government should be placed on exactly the same footing as the Canadian Pacific Railway or other great corporations, but none the less, after the expression of opinion we have had in this House, some measure should be devised for subjecting civil servants to the same obligations as other people, and in doing that, I believe that the government will be acting in the interests of the civil servants themselves. One employee of this government told me it would be an excellent thing for the service if the salaries were seizable, as it would enable a certain number of them, who are residing in other parts of the country, to obtain credit, which now they are unable to obtain without having to resort to that class of moneylenders known as money sharks.
DAVIS (Saskatchewan), I do not propose to give a silent vote on a question of this kind.
Six o'clock.

I did not hear what the hon. gentleman said. I was just going to say that I must agree with the principle of this resolution, I do not see why civil servants should be exempt any more than other people. They are a well paid class; their salaries, as a rule, are better than those paid to persons in commercial employment. And, as an hon. gentleman suggests to me, they are paid better than members of parliament are paid for their time, and I do not know of any legislation that protects a member of parliament from the necessity of paying his debts. In the North-west Territories, we have had a great deal of trouble on account of these officials. Officers of the government who are paid large salaries seem to get the idea that they can run in debt here and there and cannot be called upon to pay. But I contend that their creditors should be in a position to levy on their salaries to get their accounts paid. The question came up in the legislature of the North-west Territories and was discussed at considerable length. The government of the Territories notified the members of the House that if they would not push the resolution to a vote, they Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure).
would undertake to see that all the officers in the employ of the North-west Territories government should pay their debts or would dismiss them from the service. If the Federal government would take a similar position, it would meet the difficulty I believe. I do not know how many provinces have adopted this principle, except the province of Manitoba

An. hon. MEMBER. And Quebec.

I think the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) said that in Manitoba the government had taken the same position as the government of the North-west Territories-that is, if an officer of the government would not pay his debts, they would dismiss him. Whether the other provinces have adopted it or not, I think this is a proper principle.
If the Federal government are not prepared to make a statement like that made by the government of the North-west Territories and Manitoba, I think legislation should be allowed to go through, and I think we might expect in the future-

I think the hon. gentleman will have to wait awhile for the question. I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not see why the civil servants should be exempt any more than other classes of the community.

I was having a conversation with my hon. friend (Mr. Horsey). When the Bill was introduced the Prime Minister suggested that perhaps the phraseology might be amended to bring it into conformity with the Interpretation Act. The Solicitor General has prepared an amendment to meet that point, and we were discussing \#ith the promoter of the Bill as to whether he would accept that amendment, or whether he would require time to consider it. The proposition of the Solicitor General is to add a paragraph to section 7 of the Interpretation Act by inserting after the word Sovereign the word [DOT] Victoria Day,' and to make this apply to the Bills of Exchange Act. Of course that is a matter which involves some commercial considerations, as to whether this is to be a legal holiday in the sense of making it a public holiday for the government offices, or whether the banks are to be closed and so on. That is a matter of some moment. We are all agreed upon the principle of the Bill, but time might be taken to discuss these other points.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I was about to ask if the Bill would affect the banks, or contracts made by individuals.
If the suggestion of the Solicitor General were adopted it would be made a bank holiday. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Horsey) thinks he had better have time to consider it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

Very well, I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

In the absence of Mr. Stephens,
I beg to move that Bill (No. 77) to amend the Railway Act be read the second time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that said Bill be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways and Canals.
Motion agreed to.
Mr. Speaker, there is a very thin House, and I understand that it is not the desire of either side to continue this evening ; therefore I move that the House do now adjourn.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies).

speechtext: Before this motion is adopted, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if the government has come to any decision in regard to the Easter adjournment. Many members on this side of the House are anxious to know the extent of that adjournment.
I believe the intention is to adjourn on Thursday evening at six o'clock until the following Tuesday at three, unless there is a very strong expression of the House to the contrary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 8.40 p.m.
Thursday, March 28, 1901.
